n: Isaiah 13 is a “burden” (a weighty prophetic message of doom) against Babylon. Historically Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC. In scripture Babylon also symbolizes the wicked world that will fall before Christ’s coming.

f.g: Hebrew massa’ — a heavy oracle of judgment.

n: Raise a banner on a high mountain and call the armies to march through the gates of Babylon’s nobles.

f.g: Wave the hand as a signal.

n: God has commanded His consecrated warriors. The Book of Mormon reads “mine anger is not upon them that rejoice in my highness” — clarifying that God’s wrath is not against those who rejoice in Him.

f.g: Those set apart for God’s purpose — here, the armies He uses.

n: A roar of many kingdoms and nations gathering is heard in the mountains — the Lord is mustering an army for battle.
They come from far away, from the ends of the heavens — the Lord and the weapons of His wrath — to destroy the land.
Wail, for the day of the Lord is near — destruction from the Almighty.

f.w: the day of the Lord is at hand

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai; a wordplay — destruction (shod) from Shaddai.

n: Every hand goes limp and every heart melts with fear.
Terror seizes them like labor pains. They stare at each other in shock, faces flushed red.
The day of the Lord comes with fierce wrath to make the land desolate and remove sinners from it.

f.w: the day of the Lord cometh

n: Stars, sun, and moon will go dark — signs Jesus also described for the last days.
God will punish the world’s evil and humble the arrogance of the proud and ruthless.
People will become scarcer than fine gold — rarer than the gold of Ophir.

f.g: Ophir was a distant land famed for pure gold.

n: God will shake the heavens and move the earth from its place in His fierce anger.
Like hunted gazelles or sheep without a shepherd, foreigners in Babylon will flee to their own lands.
Anyone caught will be run through; those joined to the wicked will fall by the sword. The Book of Mormon reads “every one that is proud” where the KJV has “every one that is found.”

f.g: Pierced with a spear or sword.

n: The horrors of ancient warfare are described bluntly: children killed, houses plundered, wives assaulted. Isaiah does not hide what conquest meant.
God names the attackers: the Medes, who will not be bribed with silver or gold. The Medes allied with Persia to conquer Babylon.

f.g: A people of northwestern Iran, allied with Persia under Cyrus.

n: Their archers will show no mercy, even to the young.
Babylon, the glory of kingdoms and pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah.
Babylon will never again be inhabited — not even nomads or shepherds will camp there. The ancient city did gradually decline into ruins.
Only desert creatures will live there — owls, howling animals, and “satyrs,” likely wild goats or, in folk belief, desert demons.

f.g: Hebrew se‘irim — “hairy ones,” wild goats or goat-demons.

n: Jackals will howl in its palaces. Her time is near. The Book of Mormon adds a hopeful ending not in the KJV: God will destroy Babylon quickly and be merciful to His people, but the wicked will perish.

f.w: I will be merciful unto my people
f.g: This sentence is unique to the Book of Mormon.
